answer.evidence: The tall boulder has a pale lit band on top (rows 7-13, L=197 at x=12). It widens from 2 px at row 6 to 13-14 px by rows 10-16, so it reads as a rounded top plane seen from above. At row 14 the colour changes to the mid-tone stone face (L=144, then 111 at rows 18-19). The transition is soft and there is no crisp 1-row front-edge line, so the top evidence is moderate. Below it the front face runs about 30 rows, down to the base at rows 42-45. The dark right-hand columns (x=17, L=51-79) are light-direction shading on the same south face, not a receding side face. The offering at the foot (rows 38-41) is decor. The overall silhouette is a top plus a tall front face, which fits the three-quarter view for an organic rock.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small grey standing stone with a tiny orange offering at its foot. At board scale it reads clearly smaller and thinner than the 2x3-tile references. The stone shows only about 3 lightness steps (a light left face, a mid body and a dark right side), against roughly 5-6 steps in the tree canopies. The carved star mark and the moss are barely readable, and the surface has little per-stone grain or moss clumping, so it looks smooth and sticker-like. The measured 12 visible tones per tile sit between the references (7 and 29). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no literal flat fills. However, 54% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is mixed. The references have 0% neutral edges and carry tinted dark-green outlines. The rendering is cleaner but shallower than the richer reference, and it does not carry the foliage-like texture variety expected of a mossy forest landmark. A careful artist would find it thinner and flatter next to tree-d43edd.
